title: Shoshin, the beginner's mind
hookLine: the expert sees few possibilities. the beginner sees many.
carry: keep the beginner's mind; don't graduate from it

lines: A KNOT TIED WITHOUT A THOUGHT.
THE MIND THAT'S NEW AT THINGS.
cards: Shoelaces. Somebody tied a pair this morning without a thought about loops or tension or which hand goes where. Now watch a small child do it for the first time.
Tongue out. Every loop is an event. The lace slips, and it's fascinating.
Same shoes, same laces, two different experiences of the same knot. The adult is faster, and that's useful. But somewhere along the way, the knot stopped being interesting.
Back on day forty-three, a teacup overflowed to show a mind too full to learn. Today, the word it pointed to, up close.

teach.b: Shoshin is the Japanese word usually put into English as beginner's mind. First, the line that carried it.

Shunryu Suzuki, a Japanese Soto Zen teacher who taught in San Francisco, opened a collection of his talks, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, with an idea that can be paraphrased like this: a beginner's mind holds many possibilities, and an expert's holds only a few.
Second, what the expert loses. Knowing how something goes is a shortcut. You stop looking because you already know.
That saves time, and it quietly closes doors. A full mind has a hard time noticing what's actually in front of it. Third, what it isn't.
Beginner's mind isn't pretending to know nothing, or throwing skill away. It can belong to someone who's sat zazen every day for decades.
Suzuki's point, in paraphrase, was that the practice is to keep the beginner's mind, not to graduate from it. Fourth, why Zen cares.
Zen practice repeats itself on purpose: the same cushion, the same posture, the same breath. Without beginner's mind, that's a rut.
With it, each sitting can be a first sitting. It ties back to the koans, too: mu won't open for someone who already knows the answer.
On an ordinary Tuesday, beginner's mind might be as plain as listening to a friend tell a story you've heard before, and actually hearing it.

how: Zen teachers speak of beginner's mind as a way to approach each sitting and each ordinary task freshly, and students are encouraged to keep it however long they have practiced.

o: beginner's mind: meeting the familiar with open eyes
the Zen rank given to a student in their first year
forgetting everything you know to start from zero

s: beginner's mind means pretending you know nothing
it isn't throwing skill away. someone who's sat for decades can keep a beginner's mind.
in Suzuki's teaching, the practice is to keep the beginner's mind, not graduate from it
in paraphrase, that was his point: keep it.
beginner's mind is only for people new to meditation
it's for anyone. each sitting can be a first sitting.

games.q: you've made the same coffee every morning for years. today you want to try beginner's mind. what do you do?
o: make it with your eyes closed to prove you know it.
make it the usual way, but notice it as if for the first time.
throw out your method and learn coffee from scratch.
games.why: beginner's mind keeps the skill and drops the autopilot: same coffee, met with open eyes.

practice: Hold out one hand, palm up, and look at it as if you'd never seen a hand before: the lines, the color, how the fingers bend and where.

Then close your eyes and feel it from the inside, warmth, tingling, weight, and when the mind says it's just my hand, notice that voice and look again. If you'd rather, take one breath as if it were your first.

wordCard.voice: Shoshin. Beginner's mind. Meeting even the familiar with open eyes, without throwing away what you know. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the beginner's mind; don't graduate from it. Skill kept, door left open. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.
